    // Corner enumeration is left out: it needs an 8- (or 4-) element array

    //==
    // # Derived functionality for intervals
    //
    // Bodies for the `IInterval<T>` interface declared in
    // `intervals-bounds.concepts.plato`, plus the two concrete specializations that
    // the generic surface cannot reach: the NumberInterval remap kit (which needs
    // T/T division) and the wrap-aware AngleInterval helpers (which must survive the
    // +/-pi seam).
    //
    // Design notes on the interface surface:
    //   * IInterval<T> now bounds T to (IAdditive + IInterpolatable + IComparable) —
    //     every concrete instance (Number, Angle, Length, Integer) satisfies it, and
    //     those are the only capabilities used on T here.
    //   * Directed intervals: Contains/Overlaps/Union/Intersection/Clamp assume the
    //     forward orientation Start <= End. Use IsForward to test, Reverse to fix.
    //   * Interval-returning transforms return `Self`, not `IInterval<T>`: they are
    //     shape-preserving, so a NumberInterval in yields a NumberInterval out. The
    //     tuple bodies below build the receiver's own concrete type, which `Self` names
    //     and `IInterval<T>` does not — the interface cannot say WHICH implementer a
    //     tuple becomes, so declaring it there is both wrong for callers (they lose the
    //     concrete type) and unresolvable for the checker (CHK101 Tuple2<T,T> vs
    //     IInterval<T>). Same convention as ThenTransform in
    //     intervals.library.plato and the Deformable surface.

    //==
    // IInterval<T> — a directed one-dimensional span from Start to End
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(mathematics)).
    // T is used only through IAdditive (Add/Subtract), IInterpolatable (Lerp), and
    // IComparable (LessThanOrEquals / Lesser / Greater / Clamp), the capabilities
    // shared by every concrete interval element type (Number, Angle, Length,
    // Integer). The comparison helpers (Lesser/Greater/Clamp) come from P1
    // (core.library.plato), which derives them for any IOrderable. The interface now
    // states the bound explicitly: IInterval<T> where T: IAdditive,
    // IInterpolatable, IComparable.

    // The signed span from Start to End (End - Start); negative for a reversed
    // interval. Named Extent to avoid confusion with area/volume Size.
    Extent(self: IInterval<$T>): $T
        => self.End - self.Start;

    // True when the interval is stored in forward orientation (Start <= End).
    IsForward(self: IInterval<$T>): Boolean
        => self.Start.LessThanOrEquals(self.End);

    // True when the interval is stored reversed (Start > End).
    IsReversed(self: IInterval<$T>): Boolean
        => self.IsForward.Not;

    // The point a fraction `t` of the way from Start to End. t is unclamped:
    // 0 yields Start, 1 yields End, values outside [0,1] extrapolate
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_interpolation).
    Lerp(self: IInterval<$T>, t: Number): $T
        => self.Start.Lerp(self.End, t);

    // The midpoint of the interval.
    Center(self: IInterval<$T>): $T
        => self.Lerp(0.5);

    // True when `value` lies within the closed interval [Start, End] (both
    // endpoints inclusive). Assumes forward orientation; Reverse a reversed span.
    Contains(self: IInterval<$T>, value: $T): Boolean
        => self.Start <= value && value <= self.End;

    // True when `other` lies entirely within this closed interval (endpoints
    // inclusive). Forward orientation on both.
    ContainsInterval(self: IInterval<$T>, other: IInterval<$T>): Boolean
        => self.Contains(other.Start) && self.Contains(other.End);

    // True when the two closed intervals share any point, endpoints inclusive
    // (touching at a single endpoint counts). Closed-form; assumes forward
    // orientation on both.
    Overlaps(self: IInterval<$T>, other: IInterval<$T>): Boolean
        => self.Start <= other.End && other.Start <= self.End;

    // Restrict `value` to the closed interval [Start, End]. Assumes forward
    // orientation. Uses P1's Clamp(IOrderable, lower, upper).
    Clamp(self: IInterval<$T>, value: $T): $T
        => value.Clamp(self.Start, self.End);

    // The smallest interval containing both operands (the convex hull of the two).
    // Forward orientation: start at the lesser start, end at the greater end.
    Union(self: IInterval<$T>, other: IInterval<$T>): Self
        => (self.Start.Lesser(other.Start), self.End.Greater(other.End));

    // The overlapping interval common to both. Forward orientation: start at the
    // greater start, end at the lesser end. Empty (Start > End) when they are
    // disjoint — test with IsForward.
    Intersection(self: IInterval<$T>, other: IInterval<$T>): Self
        => (self.Start.Greater(other.Start), self.End.Lesser(other.End));

    // The same span traversed in the opposite direction (End becomes Start).
    Reverse(self: IInterval<$T>): Self
        => (self.End, self.Start);

    // The interval shifted so it starts at `start`, keeping the same extent.
    StartAt(self: IInterval<$T>, start: $T): Self
        => (start, start + self.Extent);

    // The interval translated by `delta`, moving both endpoints together.
    Translate(self: IInterval<$T>, delta: $T): Self
        => (self.Start + delta, self.End + delta);

    // The interval grown symmetrically by `amount` at each end (negative shrinks).
    Grow(self: IInterval<$T>, amount: $T): Self
        => (self.Start - amount, self.End + amount);

    // The leading sub-span from Start up to fraction `t`.
    Prefix(self: IInterval<$T>, t: Number): Self
        => (self.Start, self.Lerp(t));

    // The trailing sub-span from fraction `t` to End.
    Suffix(self: IInterval<$T>, t: Number): Self
        => (self.Lerp(t), self.End);

    // The first half of the interval.
    FirstHalf(self: IInterval<$T>): Self
        => self.Prefix(0.5);

    // The second half of the interval.
    SecondHalf(self: IInterval<$T>): Self
        => self.Suffix(0.5);

    // The sub-interval covering fractions `startFraction`..`endFraction` of this one.
    Subinterval(self: IInterval<$T>, startFraction: Number, endFraction: Number): Self
        => (self.Lerp(startFraction), self.Lerp(endFraction));

    // Split at fraction `t` into the leading and trailing sub-spans.
    SplitAt(self: IInterval<$T>, t: Number): Tuple2<Self, Self>
        => (self.Prefix(t), self.Suffix(t));

    // Split into two equal halves.
    Split(self: IInterval<$T>): Tuple2<Self, Self>
        => self.SplitAt(0.5);

    // TODO(interface-gap): Normalize (inverse Lerp: value -> fraction) is not
    // derivable here — it needs T/T division, which only Number supports among the
    // interval element types (Angle/Length/Integer are not IDivisible by Self).
    // The NumberInterval-specialized ParameterOf below fills exactly this gap.

    //==
    // NumberInterval — the remap primitive.
    // The generic IInterval surface above gives every interval Lerp/Clamp/Extent,
    // but the inverse map (value -> parameter) needs T/T division, which only Number
    // supports. NumberInterval therefore carries the three-function remap kit
    // At / ParameterOf / Clamp; Remap composes the first two across a
    // pair of intervals. Clamp(interval, value) is already inherited generically from
    // IInterval (see above), so it is not re-declared here (LIBRARIES.md rule 11).

    // The value a fraction `t` of the way from Start to End (forward lerp). The
    // remap-primitive spelling of the inherited IInterval.Lerp; 0 yields Start,
    // 1 yields End, and t outside [0,1] extrapolates.
    At(self: NumberInterval, t: Number): Number
        => self.Lerp(t);
